title: Bereshit: walking with God (Genesis 5:24)
hookLine: among long lists of generations, Enoch "walked with God, and he was not"

lines: A LIST OF NAMES YOU SKIM.
AND HE DIED. AND HE DIED.
cards: Some families keep a list like this: a page in the front of an old Bible, a spreadsheet a cousin made, a chart on a genealogy site. Names, dates, who begat whom. Most of it gets skimmed.
Genesis chapter five is that list, from Adam to Noah. Each man is born, has a son, lives so many years, has other sons and daughters. And then, again and again, the same closing words: and he died.
And he died. And he died. Like a drumbeat.
Until one name, where the drumbeat breaks.

teach.h: AND HE DIED. AND HE DIED.
teach.b: His name is Enoch, seventh from Adam.

teach.h: ENOCH WALKED WITH GOD, AND WAS NOT.
teach.b: Instead of and he died, the Torah says: "And Enoch walked with God, and he was not; for God took him." One verse, and he's gone. The Torah doesn't explain it.
What does he was not mean?

The rabbis disagree. The midrash records a debate: some teachers read it as praise, others as something more complicated. Rashi says Enoch was righteous, but easily swayed, so God took him early, before he could go wrong.

Enoch lived three hundred sixty-five years, far fewer than the others on the list. Other ancient Jewish writings, outside the Hebrew Bible, told great stories of Enoch rising to heaven. The Torah itself says only this.
Now the verb, walked. In Hebrew it's vayithalech, a form that can mean walked about, kept walking.
Some readers hear in it a way of life, not a single trip: going through the days with God alongside. The phrase comes back soon, about another man; you'll hear it tomorrow.
And that's the first portion, Bereshit, finished. A letter open ahead. Creation told twice.
One person, a whole world. An urge you can rule. And, in a long list of names, one man who walked with God.
The portion ends on a quiet line: "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." A door, open ahead, into the next portion.

how: Jewish readers study the genealogies of Genesis 5 with Rashi and the midrash, and 'walking with God' is often taught as a picture of a steady, everyday religious life.

games.q: you're reading Genesis 5: and he died, and he died. you reach Enoch. what does the Torah say instead?
o: and he was king over the earth.
and he walked with God, and he was not.
games.why: "And Enoch walked with God, and he was not; for God took him." the drumbeat breaks, and the Torah doesn't explain.

practice: Imagine walking at an easy pace down a quiet road, one step with each breath in, one with each breath out.
If you pray, picture God walking beside you; if you don't, picture whatever you most want beside you on the road: goodness, patience, someone you love. Don't hurry; just keep walking.

wordCard.voice: Bereshit. The first portion: from the first letter to Enoch, who walked with God, to Noah, who found grace.

orig.note: Hebrew: and he walked about; a form some readers hear as ongoing walking.
